floor_history.note: Floor holds at 7/91 (live). Kill re-audit: the do{}while(0) FAKE is load-bearing (7 vs 17 hand-ablated), so every s21-s24 kill stands. s24's central claim is CORRECTED: the inline form carries target's instruction multiset but NOT its dependence graph - sched_solver (model order- and clock-exact at baseline) finds no vector at depth 1 over all 1332 atoms nor depth 2 over the spellable ones, target's order is not a fixed point, and the reachable set under statement reordering is 32 emissions of which the best satisfies 9 of 13 target constraints. New axis opened: the arg4 ADDRESS-POINTER local is the first spelling ever to put arg4's value load at the register-load point (target's geometry), but a pointer-typed expression flips the addu to base-first where target is index-first, excluding the whole family on operand order.

frontier.hypothesis: Target's window needs a longer critical path through arg4's chain and a shorter one through arg5's, while every argument stays an inline subscript so the addu stays index-first. The four unbought constraints are priority inversions, and priority is a pure function of the dependence graph.
frontier.mechanism: s25 measured that statement order is exhausted on the inline graph (32 reachable emissions, best 9/13). rank_for_schedule sorts priority-descending before any tie-break, so those four orderings can only be bought by changing the graph. Concretely target needs p(arg4.lbu) above p(arg5.lbu) while p(arg4.sll) stays below p(arg5.sll) - an edge strictly between arg4's lbu and its sll - and it needs the stack store (121) to fall below arg3's addu (101).
frontier.next_probe: Reuse tmp/grind/CD_datasync/s25/luid_search.py as the harness but perturb the GRAPH instead of the LUIDs: enumerate single add_dep/del_dep atoms on the inline pass-1 block 3, recompute priorities with perturb.apply_priorities, and re-run the LUID search for each, scoring the 13 constraints. Report every atom that lifts the best score above 9, and for each name the C construct that would place that edge. This converts 'which edge' from a guess into a bounded enumeration, and s25 proved it is the right question.

frontier.hypothesis: The stack-argument store's position (UID 121) is a separate, independently movable lever: target emits sw 16($sp) at window slot 12, after arg3's addu, where every measured form emits it by slot 9.
frontier.mechanism: 121 has priority 3 and both register-argument loads (127, 129) depend on it, so it is scheduled early in every reachable order. Target's late store implies the two loads do not both depend on it - i.e. target's memory-dependence structure between the stack store and the two table loads differs from ours. That is a C-level aliasing question, not an ordering one.
frontier.next_probe: Ask whether del_dep 127<-121, del_dep 129<-121, or both lifts the reachable-set score with the same harness. If it does, the C question is what makes GCC 2.7.2's sched.c prove the stack store independent of the two table loads - candidates: the tables reached through differently-typed pointers, or a fifth argument whose store does not alias an s32 load. Always recompile to verify; the model proposes, the compiler disposes.

frontier.hypothesis: The twins CD_sync and CD_ready share this window, so the s25 role map and the graph-perturbation result transfer and the enumeration only has to be run once.
frontier.mechanism: CD_ready s36/s46 record a byte-shape-IDENTICAL do_timeout window and CD_sync s26 records the same {sll,addu,sll} -> jal debug_printf residual. s25's finding is a statement about the block's dependence graph and priorities, which are properties of the shared source idiom rather than of CD_datasync's chassis.
frontier.next_probe: Run tools/sched_solver/extract.py on the twins' best banked forms and build the same role map. If their pass-1 block priorities match CD_datasync's, one graph answer closes three functions; if a twin's priorities differ, that difference is a lever CD_datasync does not have and is worth importing.
